newsitem.title: MEXICO: Clinton begins state visit to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Clinton begins state visit to Mexico.

text.p: President Bill Clinton arrived in Mexico on Monday for a state visit to the United States' third biggest trading partner -- and its main supplier of illegal drugs and immigrants.

Clinton emerged from Air Force One into the evening air to be greeted briefly by Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria. He then walked across the concrete apron on crutches to board a helicopter for a short hop across the city to his hotel.

Waiting at the National Anthropology Museum to greet Clinton was Mexican president Ernesto Zedillo, who showed his visitor a priceless Aztec calendar carved in stone during an informal encounter ahead of the official programme starting Tuesday.
"It's quite gorgeous," enthused Clinton to waiting reporters.

Security was exceptionally tight in the Mexican capital for the visit, with hundreds of troops and police sealing off streets around the area Clinton was to occupy and searching cars and passers-by. Rooftop snipers also stood guard.

The mood in the smoggy Mexican capital was subdued. Most citizens were off work celebrating the 135th anniversary of a famed battle that repelled French invaders and there were few spontaneous signs of welcome for the U.S. president.

A group of left-wing protesters waved "Clinton Go Home" banners in the central Chapultepec Park and a debtor's group briefly attached a black ribbon to an independence monument saying Clinton's arrival was an "insult to the homeland".
Police scuffled with several hundred teachers attempting to march on the U.S. embassy and burning the American flag but there were no reports of serious violence.

Clinton was the first American president to visit the Mexican capital since Jimmy Carter in 1979. He was also making his first trip to Latin America since taking power in 1993, a journey that will take in Costa Rica and Barbados for summits with regional leaders later in the week.

Fearful of arousing popular anti-American sentiment, the Mexican government avoided lining the president's route with Stars and Stripes flags and used an ambiguous red, white and blue striped design instead.
Thanks to the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) that entered force in 1994, the two countries saw bilateral trade surge to a record $140 billion last year.

Both sides say government-to-government cooperation is also at record levels -- something borne out by the 12 U.S. cabinet or cabinet-level officials who attended a meeting on Monday afternoon of the U.S.-Mexico Binational Commission to discuss a wide range of bilateral concerns.
But dominating Clinton's agenda were the perennial thorns in the sides of both nations -- drugs and immigration.

Senior officials from both sides made a plea on Monday for cooperation rather than confrontation in the struggle to stop the flow of cocaine, heroin and marijuana across the border from Mexico into the United States.
"On the drug issue, a lot of people maybe feel that we are sometimes making comments that impinge on sovereignty," Clinton told Mexican television just before leaving Washington.

"All I can say is that the United States has a big drug problem and we expect to take responsibility. Every country that has been infiltrated significantly by drugs soon pays an enormous price for it. So I see this as a joint struggle between Mexico and the United States."
U.S. ambassador to Mexico James Jones warned in an interview with Newsweek magazine that Mexico could become "another Colombia" if it did not act swiftly against drug traffickers.
And Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said the two nations still had a long way to go before they could declare victory in the drug war.

"We know that in the struggle between law and outlaw, between democratic integrity and corrupt expediency we are neither winning nor losing, but remain in the hottest stages of battle," Albright told the Binational Commission.
Republic Sen. Phil Gramm of Texas urged Clinton to complain to Mexico about narcotics corruption and the "river of drugs and death that continues to flow from Mexico into Texas."

But Mexican Foreign Minister Gurria told the Binational Commission meeting that only drug traffickers would benefit if the two nations squabbled "in a sterile and irritating exercise of allocating blame."
Clinton's wife Hillary faced a different kind of problem on her tour of ancient Maya ruins in southern Mexico.
The first lady said she was unable to scale the famed Uxmal pyramid because she wore the wrong shoes.
